patient.chief_complaint: Fluctuating diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia with unusual anticoagulation history
patient.hpi:
A 44-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted to the neurology ward for evaluation of fluctuating diplopia, bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, dysphonia, and fatigable chewing. Symptoms were characteristically worse at the end of meals and at the end of the day, and improved significantly with rest. She had noticed progressive worsening over 8 weeks, with diplopia initially present only on right lateral gaze, subsequently becoming present throughout the day. She described difficulty chewing through a full meal without tiring, nasal voice quality when reading aloud for more than a few minutes, and increasing difficulty swallowing pills over the past 2 weeks.

Her past medical history was notable for antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), diagnosed 6 years ago following three consecutive spontaneous first-trimester abortions. She also had a history of transient hypothyroidism following a viral illness 4 years ago that resolved without treatment. She was taking aspirin 81 mg daily for APS-related thromboprophylaxis. She had no prior neurological diagnosis.

On examination, she demonstrated progressive fatigability of upward gaze during a prolonged Simpson test. Ptosis was bilaterally present (left greater than right) and worsened with sustained upgaze. She had dysarthria and weakness of facial and neck muscles. Tongue strength was mildly reduced but symmetric. The Cogan lid twitch sign was positive. Ice pack test produced a 3 mm improvement bilaterally in 5 minutes. Limb strength was 5/5 throughout with normal coordination and sensation.

The antiphospholipid syndrome history raised initial concern for cerebrovascular disease as a possible explanatory framework — specifically, a small basilar artery TIA producing bilateral ocular motor signs. Laboratory results were notable for elevated anticardiolipin antibodies and anti-β2-glycoprotein-I antibodies consistent with her known APS, and prolonged PTT attributed to lupus anticoagulant.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Seronegative generalized myasthenia gravis, diagnosed by SFEMG, in patient with antiphospholipid syndrome

differential.key_features: APS can cause stroke or microvascular CNS events; here MRI/MRA reassuring; pattern fluctuating fatigable, not focal vascular.
APS-MS overlap is recognized; MRI here without demyelination; pattern incompatible.
MuSK-MG presents with bulbar predominance and poor RNS response; here MuSK negative on standard assay — clustered cell-based assay should be considered.
Objective SFEMG abnormalities exclude functional etiology.
No baseline CMAP reduction; no facilitation pattern.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR, MuSK, and LRP4 all negative (seronegative MG); TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No thymoma; thymic involution appropriate for age

optimal_actions.action: Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

optimal_actions.action: Bedside ice-pack test for ptosis (cheap, ~80% sensitive for ocular MG)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

optimal_actions.action: Echocardiogram to screen for Libman-Sacks endocarditis (APS-associated valvular disease)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Document valvular status given APS background

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Confirm AChR, MuSK, LRP4 all negative; pursue clustered AChR cell-based assay
Single-fiber EMG — diagnostic in seronegative MG
Coordinate steroid initiation with rheumatology and hematology — APS anticoagulation
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids in APS without coordinated anticoagulation review — thrombotic risk.
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Seronegative status (AChR, MuSK, LRP4 negative) does NOT exclude MG — proceed to single-fiber EMG; clustered cell-based AChR assays detect additional cases.
APS-MG overlap is described — both autoimmune; manage anticoagulation alongside MG immunosuppression.
Clustered AChR cell-based assays catch additional seronegative cases.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute neurological symptoms to APS cerebrovascular events.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MRI/MRA reassuring; fatigable diurnal pattern with abnormal SFEMG is MG independent of APS.

red_herrings.finding: Antiphospholipid syndrome with positive lupus anticoagulant — TIA concern
red_herrings.why_misleading: APS is a known cause of stroke and TIA; bilateral ocular motor signs + APS history creates strong anchoring to vascular diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal brain MRI/MRA excludes TIA; fatigable, diurnal symptoms are incompatible with vascular etiology

red_herrings.why_misleading: Elevated aPTT typically triggers investigation for bleeding diathesis or factor deficiency
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Elevated aPTT is from lupus anticoagulant (in vitro artifact); mixing study shows inhibitor pattern; no true coagulopathy

red_herrings.why_misleading: Negative AChR, MuSK, and LRP4 antibodies might lead clinician to abandon MG diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Seronegative MG (~15% of generalized cases); SFEMG is the required next step with >97% sensitivity

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Fatigable ocular motor and bulbar signs

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS at orbicularis oculi, abductor digiti minimi, deltoid

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi (facial nerve): Decrement 17% (1st to 4th stimulus) [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Abductor digiti minimi (ulnar nerve): Decrement 13% ABNORMAL
  Deltoid: Decrement 10% BORDERLINE ABNORMAL

IMPRESSION: Decremental responses at 3 Hz in cranial, distal, and proximal muscles, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: RNS: 17% decrement orbicularis, 13% abductor digiti minimi, 10% deltoid — decremental pattern in cranial and limb muscles, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.interpretation: AChR binding antibody below detection threshold (<0.4 nmol/L). AChR blocking antibody negative. Anti-MuSK antibody negative. Anti-LRP4 antibody negative. All tested acetylcholine receptor and related antibodies are within normal limits. A negative result does not exclude a disorder of neuromuscular transmission; clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Clinical literature
results.content:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Antiphospholipid Syndrome and Myasthenia Gravis Co-occurrence

KEY FINDINGS:
1. APS-MG ASSOCIATION: Co-occurrence of APS and MG is documented in the literature; both are autoimmune conditions that can co-exist in polyautoimmune individuals.
2. SERONEGATIVE MG IN POLYAUTOIMMUNE CONTEXT: Patients with APS/SLE may have higher rates of antibody-negative NMJ disease; extended antibody panels may detect additional targets not routinely tested.
3. LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT AND LABORATORY COAGULATION TESTS: Lupus anticoagulant prolongs aPTT in vitro as a laboratory artifact; mixing studies typically show an inhibitor pattern.
4. THYMECTOMY IN ANTIBODY-NEGATIVE MG: Evidence from the MGTX trial focused on AChR-positive patients; benefit in seronegative disease is less established.
5. IMMUNOSUPPRESSION IN MG: Prednisone and azathioprine are established first-line agents. Mycophenolate mofetil is an alternative.

output.summary: APS and MG can co-exist in polyautoimmune patients; lupus anticoagulant prolongs aPTT as an in-vitro artifact; single-fiber EMG is the most sensitive test for NMJ dysfunction when antibodies are negative.

interactions:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — PREDNISONE AND AZATHIOPRINE WITH ASPIRIN

Query: Corticosteroid and azathioprine co-administration with aspirin

FINDINGS:
  PREDNISONE + ASPIRIN:
  - Additive GI mucosal irritation risk; gastroprotection (e.g., PPI) recommended when used concurrently
  - Corticosteroids can cause transient worsening of neuromuscular disease at initiation; slow titration is advised

  AZATHIOPRINE + ASPIRIN:
  - No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction
  - Azathioprine may have mild antiplatelet properties; platelet count monitoring recommended
  - Myelosuppression monitoring required (CBC monthly for 3 months, then quarterly)
  - TPMT genotyping recommended before initiating azathioprine to assess myelosuppression risk

  AZATHIOPRINE + WARFARIN (if co-prescribed):
  - Azathioprine may modestly reduce warfarin effect; INR monitoring frequency should increase if warfarin is added
warnings: GI protection recommended when combining prednisone + aspirin; TPMT genotyping before azathioprine; CBC monitoring required; monitor INR if warfarin co-prescribed.
